title: How Buffett wound down his partnership: BPL letters, 1967-1970
summary: Buffett's letters track BPL's results, then explain why he cut his goals in 1967 and liquidated in 1969 as bargains vanished and speculation grew. He covers quantitative versus qualitative investing, ignoring market price for controlled businesses, and a plain-spoken guide to tax-free bonds.

principles.text: Sure money comes from obvious quantitative bargains; the big money comes from rare high-probability qualitative insights.
principles.quote: So the really big money tends to be made by investors who are right on qualitative decisions but, at least in my opinion, the more sure money tends to be made on the obvious quantitative decisions.

principles.text: Stick with a method you understand even when the crowd profits from a style you don't.
principles.quote: I will not abandon a previous approach whose logic I understand (although I find it difficult to apply) even though it may mean foregoing large and apparently easy, profits

principles.text: Market quotes don't set the value of a business you control; operating performance does.
principles.quote: Market price is irrelevant to us in the valuation of our controlling interests.

principles.text: Over time the market weighs fundamentals; short-term moves are votes driven by psychology, and fundamentals are easier to judge.
principles.quote: I have always found it easier to evaluate weights dictated by fundamentals than votes dictated by psychology.

principles.text: Stay inside your circle of competence and pass on what you can't analyze; just be right on what you do choose.
principles.quote: My approach to bonds is pretty much like my approach to stocks. If I can't understand something, I tend to forget it.

principles.text: He valued people and human consequences over a few extra points of return, even in a weak business.
principles.quote: I have no desire to trade severe human dislocations for a few percentage points additional return per annum.
